    <!-- Page label -->
    <text x="60" y="55" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="500" fill="#D97757" letter-spacing="2">CONCLUSIONS</text>

    <!-- Page title -->
    <text x="640" y="110" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF" text-anchor="middle">Key Takeaways: Design Principles for</text>
    <text x="640" y="148" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF" text-anchor="middle">Efficient Multimodal Models</text>

    <!-- Decorative divider -->
    <rect x="540" y="165" width="200" height="3" fill="url(#accentGradient)" rx="1.5"/>

    <!-- Five takeaways in two rows -->
    <!-- Row 1: 3 cards -->
    <!-- Card 1 -->
    <rect x="60" y="200" width="370" height="200" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.05" stroke="#FFFFFF" stroke-opacity="0.1" stroke-width="1"/>
    <rect x="60" y="200" width="370" height="5" fill="#10B981" rx="2"/>

    <circle cx="110" cy="250" r="22" fill="#10B981" fill-opacity="0.2"/>
    <text x="110" y="257" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#10B981" text-anchor="middle">1</text>

    <text x="145" y="255" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">Balance Encoder-LM Compute</text>

    <text x="90" y="295" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">Smaller vision encoders serve compact</text>
    <text x="90" y="315" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">VLMs better. The 93M SigLIP-B/16</text>
    <text x="90" y="335" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">outperforms 428M SigLIP-SO400M for</text>
    <text x="90" y="355" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">small LMs.</text>

    <rect x="460" y="200" width="370" height="200" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.05" stroke="#FFFFFF" stroke-opacity="0.1" stroke-width="1"/>
    <rect x="460" y="200" width="370" height="5" fill="#4A90D9" rx="2"/>

    <circle cx="510" cy="250" r="22" fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.2"/>
    <text x="510" y="257" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#4A90D9" text-anchor="middle">2</text>

    <text x="545" y="255" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">Extend Context Length</text>

    <text x="490" y="295" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">Extending from 2K to 16K tokens</text>
    <text x="490" y="315" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">unlocks higher image resolution and</text>
    <text x="490" y="335" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">significant performance gains via RoPE</text>
    <text x="490" y="355" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">base adjustment (10K → 273K).</text>

    <rect x="860" y="200" width="370" height="200" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.05" stroke="#FFFFFF" stroke-opacity="0.1" stroke-width="1"/>
    <rect x="860" y="200" width="370" height="5" fill="#D97757" rx="2"/>

    <text x="945" y="255" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">Aggressive Token Compression</text>

    <text x="890" y="295" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">Pixel shuffle at r=4 gives 16x token</text>
    <text x="890" y="315" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">reduction for small models, easing</text>
    <text x="890" y="335" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">attention overhead and improving</text>
    <text x="890" y="355" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">long-context modeling.</text>

    <!-- Row 2: 2 cards centered -->

    <rect x="160" y="430" width="440" height="200" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.05" stroke="#FFFFFF" stroke-opacity="0.1" stroke-width="1"/>
    <rect x="160" y="430" width="440" height="5" fill="#10B981" rx="2"/>

    <circle cx="210" cy="480" r="22" fill="#10B981" fill-opacity="0.2"/>
    <text x="210" y="487" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#10B981" text-anchor="middle">4</text>

    <text x="245" y="485" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">Sub-1GB Inference Is Achievable</text>

    <text x="190" y="520" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">SmolVLM-256M runs in only 0.8 GB GPU RAM,</text>
    <text x="190" y="540" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">enabling deployment on smartphones and</text>
    <text x="190" y="560" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">low-power edge devices with real-time</text>
    <text x="190" y="580" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">throughput (~80 tok/s on Apple Silicon).</text>

    <!-- Card 5 -->
    <rect x="640" y="430" width="440" height="200" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.05" stroke="#FFFFFF" stroke-opacity="0.1" stroke-width="1"/>
    <rect x="640" y="430" width="440" height="5" fill="#D97757" rx="2"/>

    <circle cx="690" cy="480" r="22" fill="#D97757" fill-opacity="0.2"/>
    <text x="690" y="487" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#D97757" text-anchor="middle">5</text>

    <text x="725" y="485" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">Fully Open-Source Release</text>

    <text x="670" y="520" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">All model weights, training datasets, code,</text>
    <text x="670" y="540" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">and the HuggingSnap mobile app are fully</text>
    <text x="670" y="560" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">open-sourced to promote reproducibility</text>
    <text x="670" y="580" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">and on-device AI research.</text>

    <!-- Bottom call to action -->
    <text x="640" y="670" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.5" text-anchor="middle">Architectural efficiency matters more than raw scale for edge deployment.</text>

    <!-- Page number -->
    <text x="640" y="695" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.3" text-anchor="middle">9 / 9</text>
</svg>

# 01_cover

Welcome to our presentation on SmolVLM, a family of compact vision-language models that redefine what's possible for on-device multimodal AI. [Pause]

SmolVLM achieves competitive benchmark performance with dramatically lower memory footprints — the smallest model runs in just 0.8 GB of GPU RAM, yet outperforms models 300 times its size. This is made possible through three key architectural innovations we'll walk through today.

Key points: 1) Sub-1GB inference for VLMs 2) Competitive performance at 300x smaller 3) Three architectural innovations
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_problem

[Transition] Let's start by understanding why we need SmolVLM in the first place.

State-of-the-art vision-language models are powerful, but they're fundamentally impractical for edge deployment. Molmo-A1B-7B requires 27.7 GB of GPU RAM — that's a datacenter requirement, not a mobile device. [Data] Idefics-80B has 80 billion parameters. These models simply cannot run on smartphones or edge devices.

The core tension is that cloud-dependent VLMs can't serve privacy-sensitive or latency-critical applications. SmolVLM addresses this with three model sizes — 256M at 0.8 GB, 500M at 1.2 GB, and 2.2B at 4.9 GB — all achievable on consumer hardware. [Pause]

Key points: 1) SOTA VLMs require 27.7+ GB RAM 2) SmolVLM-256M outperforms 300x larger Idefics-80B 3) Three architectural innovations enable this efficiency
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_architecture

[Transition] Now let's look under the hood at how SmolVLM achieves this efficiency.

The architecture follows a clear pipeline: images are first split into sub-images, then encoded by a SigLIP vision encoder, compressed via pixel shuffle, projected through a linear layer into the SmolLM2 language model's input space, and finally concatenated with text token embeddings. [Data] For video, frames are sampled and processed through the same pipeline.

Three key steps drive the design: image splitting handles high-resolution inputs, the encode-and-compress stage uses SigLIP plus pixel shuffle for dramatic token reduction, and the SmolLM2 backbone generates the final output across three sizes.

Key points: 1) Clean pipeline: split, encode, compress, project, generate 2) Pixel shuffle provides 4x or 16x token reduction 3) Three LM sizes: 135M, 360M, 1.7B
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_compute_allocation

[Transition] The first critical finding is about compute allocation — and it's counterintuitive.

For compact VLMs, a smaller vision encoder actually outperforms a larger one. [Data] The 93M SigLIP-B/16 paired with a 135M LM delivers better results than the 428M SigLIP-SO400M with the same LM. [Pause]

Only at the 1.7B LM scale does the larger encoder justify its 10% parameter overhead. The implication is clear: don't over-provision the encoder for small language models. Balanced compute allocation matters more than raw encoder size.

Key points: 1) 93M encoder beats 428M encoder for small LMs 2) Scale crossover at 1.7B LM 3) Balanced allocation > raw encoder size
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_token_compression

[Transition] The second key finding concerns how aggressively we can compress visual tokens.

Pixel shuffle is a space-to-depth operation that rearranges spatial features into channels, reducing token count by r squared. At r=4, this gives a 16x token reduction — which is dramatic. [Data] Small VLMs benefit most from this aggressive compression because it eases attention overhead and frees capacity for the language model backbone.

Larger models prefer r=2 with only 4x reduction, preserving spatial detail that their larger LMs can process. The key insight is that the optimal compression factor depends on model size.

Key points: 1) r=4 gives 16x token reduction for small models 2) r=2 preserves detail for larger models 3) Compression factor should match model capacity
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_context_length

[Transition] The third finding addresses context length — a critical enabler for image resolution.

Extending context from 2K to 16K tokens produces significant performance improvements across all model sizes. [Data] This was achieved by adjusting the RoPE base from 10K to 273K and fine-tuning on mixed long and short-context data. The 2.2B model uses the full 16K context, while the smaller 256M and 500M variants use 8K.

More context means more tokens for visual detail, which directly translates to higher effective image resolution. This is a straightforward but powerful architectural choice.

Key points: 1) 2K to 16K tokens unlocks higher resolution 2) RoPE base 10K to 273K 3) 2.2B uses 16K; 256M/500M use 8K
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_benchmarks

[Transition] Let's now look at the full benchmark picture across 13 benchmarks.

SmolVLM was evaluated on single-image understanding, multi-task reasoning, and video comprehension. [Benchmark] The 2.2B model achieves 59.8% average, rivaling state-of-the-art models that consume twice the GPU memory. [Data] Notably, SmolVLM-2.2B outperforms the best efficient open-source baselines on 7 out of 11 benchmarks, including OCRBench, ChartQA, TextVQA, DocVQA, ScienceQA, MMMU, MathVista, and both video benchmarks.

The RAM comparison tells the real story: SmolVLM-256M uses 0.8 GB versus Molmo-A1B-7B's 27.7 GB — a 35x reduction in memory for a model that still surpasses the 300x larger Idefics-80B. [Pause]

Key points: 1) 59.8% average for 2.2B model 2) 7/11 benchmarks beat efficient OS baselines 3) 35x less RAM than comparable baselines
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 08_on_device

[Transition] Performance benchmarks are one thing — real-world deployment is another. Let's look at on-device results.

SmolVLM runs on-device via the HuggingSnap iOS app, processing photos and videos entirely locally with zero cloud dependency. [Data] On a MacBook Pro M1 Max 64GB, the 256M model achieves up to 80 tokens per second at batch size 1. Even on a MacBook Air M3 with just 16 GB, it delivers approximately 55 tokens per second.

At batch size 64, throughput reaches nearly 1000 tokens per second on high-end devices. [Pause] This means real-time multimodal inference on consumer hardware is not a future promise — it's available today.

Key points: 1) Up to 80 tok/s on Apple Silicon 2) HuggingSnap: fully local, no cloud 3) ~1000 tok/s at batch=64 on high-end devices
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 09_takeaways

[Transition] Let me close with five actionable design principles from our work.

First, balance encoder-LM compute — smaller encoders serve compact VLMs better. Second, extend context length — going from 2K to 16K tokens unlocks higher image resolution. Third, use aggressive token compression for small models — r=4 gives 16x reduction. Fourth, sub-1GB inference is achievable — we've demonstrated it with SmolVLM-256M. Fifth, everything is fully open-sourced — weights, data, code, and the mobile app. [Pause]

The core message: architectural efficiency matters more than raw scale for edge deployment. SmolVLM proves that carefully designed compact models can rival much larger systems while running on the devices people already own.

Key points: 1) Balance compute allocation 2) Extend context 3) Compress aggressively for small models 4) Sub-1GB is achievable 5) Fully open-source
Duration: 2 minutes

[Transition] Now let's look under the hood at how SmolVLM achieves this efficiency.

The architecture follows a clear pipeline: images are first split into sub-images, then encoded by a SigLIP vision encoder, compressed via pixel shuffle, projected through a linear layer into the SmolLM2 language model's input space, and finally concatenated with text token embeddings. [Data] For video, frames are sampled and processed through the same pipeline.

Three key steps drive the design: image splitting handles high-resolution inputs, the encode-and-compress stage uses SigLIP plus pixel shuffle for dramatic token reduction, and the SmolLM2 backbone generates the final output across three sizes.

Key points: 1) Clean pipeline: split, encode, compress, project, generate 2) Pixel shuffle provides 4x or 16x token reduction 3) Three LM sizes: 135M, 360M, 1.7B
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_compute_allocation

[Transition] The first critical finding is about compute allocation — and it's counterintuitive.

For compact VLMs, a smaller vision encoder actually outperforms a larger one. [Data] The 93M SigLIP-B/16 paired with a 135M LM delivers better results than the 428M SigLIP-SO400M with the same LM. [Pause]

Only at the 1.7B LM scale does the larger encoder justify its 10% parameter overhead. The implication is clear: don't over-provision the encoder for small language models. Balanced compute allocation matters more than raw encoder size.

Key points: 1) 93M encoder beats 428M encoder for small LMs 2) Scale crossover at 1.7B LM 3) Balanced allocation > raw encoder size
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_token_compression

[Transition] The second key finding concerns how aggressively we can compress visual tokens.

Pixel shuffle is a space-to-depth operation that rearranges spatial features into channels, reducing token count by r squared. At r=4, this gives a 16x token reduction — which is dramatic. [Data] Small VLMs benefit most from this aggressive compression because it eases attention overhead and frees capacity for the language model backbone.

Larger models prefer r=2 with only 4x reduction, preserving spatial detail that their larger LMs can process. The key insight is that the optimal compression factor depends on model size.

Key points: 1) r=4 gives 16x token reduction for small models 2) r=2 preserves detail for larger models 3) Compression factor should match model capacity
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_context_length

[Transition] The third finding addresses context length — a critical enabler for image resolution.

Extending context from 2K to 16K tokens produces significant performance improvements across all model sizes. [Data] This was achieved by adjusting the RoPE base from 10K to 273K and fine-tuning on mixed long and short-context data. The 2.2B model uses the full 16K context, while the smaller 256M and 500M variants use 8K.

More context means more tokens for visual detail, which directly translates to higher effective image resolution. This is a straightforward but powerful architectural choice.

Key points: 1) 2K to 16K tokens unlocks higher resolution 2) RoPE base 10K to 273K 3) 2.2B uses 16K; 256M/500M use 8K
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_benchmarks

[Transition] Let's now look at the full benchmark picture across 13 benchmarks.

SmolVLM was evaluated on single-image understanding, multi-task reasoning, and video comprehension. [Benchmark] The 2.2B model achieves 59.8% average, rivaling state-of-the-art models that consume twice the GPU memory. [Data] Notably, SmolVLM-2.2B outperforms the best efficient open-source baselines on 7 out of 11 benchmarks, including OCRBench, ChartQA, TextVQA, DocVQA, ScienceQA, MMMU, MathVista, and both video benchmarks.

The RAM comparison tells the real story: SmolVLM-256M uses 0.8 GB versus Molmo-A1B-7B's 27.7 GB — a 35x reduction in memory for a model that still surpasses the 300x larger Idefics-80B. [Pause]

Key points: 1) 59.8% average for 2.2B model 2) 7/11 benchmarks beat efficient OS baselines 3) 35x less RAM than comparable baselines
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 08_on_device

[Transition] Performance benchmarks are one thing — real-world deployment is another. Let's look at on-device results.

SmolVLM runs on-device via the HuggingSnap iOS app, processing photos and videos entirely locally with zero cloud dependency. [Data] On a MacBook Pro M1 Max 64GB, the 256M model achieves up to 80 tokens per second at batch size 1. Even on a MacBook Air M3 with just 16 GB, it delivers approximately 55 tokens per second.

At batch size 64, throughput reaches nearly 1000 tokens per second on high-end devices. [Pause] This means real-time multimodal inference on consumer hardware is not a future promise — it's available today.

Key points: 1) Up to 80 tok/s on Apple Silicon 2) HuggingSnap: fully local, no cloud 3) ~1000 tok/s at batch=64 on high-end devices
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 09_takeaways

[Transition] Let me close with five actionable design principles from our work.

First, balance encoder-LM compute — smaller encoders serve compact VLMs better. Second, extend context length — going from 2K to 16K tokens unlocks higher image resolution. Third, use aggressive token compression for small models — r=4 gives 16x reduction. Fourth, sub-1GB inference is achievable — we've demonstrated it with SmolVLM-256M. Fifth, everything is fully open-sourced — weights, data, code, and the mobile app. [Pause]

The core message: architectural efficiency matters more than raw scale for edge deployment. SmolVLM proves that carefully designed compact models can rival much larger systems while running on the devices people already own.

Key points: 1) Balance compute allocation 2) Extend context 3) Compress aggressively for small models 4) Sub-1GB is achievable 5) Fully open-source
Duration: 2 minutes

steps.message:
The presentation has been generated and saved to `/app/output/final_deck.pptx` (84 KB).

**Summary of the 9-slide deck:**

1. **Cover** — Dark gradient background with title, key stats (0.8GB, 300x, 59.8%)
2. **Problem Motivation** — Two-column comparison: large VLM memory gap vs SmolVLM's edge-ready sizes, with RAM bar visualization
3. **Architecture Overview** — Horizontal pipeline diagram (Image → Splitting → SigLIP → Pixel Shuffle → Projection → SmolLM2) + three step cards
4. **Compute Allocation** — Grouped bar chart comparing 93M vs 428M encoder performance at 135M and 1.7B LM scales
5. **Token Compression** — Pixel shuffle mechanism visualization with before/after spatial-to-channel diagram, r=4 vs r=2 comparison cards
6. **Context Length Scaling** — Three cards: context extension results, technical approach (RoPE 10K→273K), model configurations (8K/16K)
7. **Benchmark Performance** — Full 11-benchmark data table with SmolVLM 256M/500M/2.2B vs best efficient OS baselines, RAM comparison sidebar
8. **On-Device Deployment** — Throughput bar chart by Apple Silicon device, HuggingSnap app details, KPI cards
9. **Key Takeaways** — Dark background with five numbered design principles
